s01: This dot can keep changing state while its probabilities settle.
At each step, the next state depends only on where it is now.
From A, it moves to B with probability one quarter.
From B, it returns to A with probability one half.
Otherwise, it stays where it is.
Now follow probabilities, not one particular path.
Suppose the chance of A is two thirds, and B is one third.
One quarter of the probability in state A moves to B: one sixth in total.
Half of the B probability moves to A: also one sixth.
Equal probability moves both ways, so the distribution stays the same.
That is a stationary distribution.
It does not mean the dot stops moving.
It means the chances of finding it in A or B do not change.
Will a different starting point approach this balance?
Start in state A with probability one.
After one step, the chance of A is three quarters.
After two steps, it is eleven sixteenths, closer to two thirds.
Call the current chance of A, p.
Next time, we keep three quarters of p, and gain half of the remaining probability.
That is one half plus one quarter of p.
Subtract two thirds from both sides: the gap from balance becomes one quarter as large each step.
So this chain approaches the same balance from any starting probability.
This conclusion uses these transition rules; not every Markov chain settles.
The motion can continue while the proportions become steady.

scenes.narration:
This dot can keep changing state while its probabilities settle. At each step, the next state depends only on where it is now. From A, it moves to B with probability one quarter. From B, it returns to A with probability one half. Otherwise, it stays where it is.

Now follow probabilities, not one particular path. Suppose the chance of A is two thirds, and B is one third. One quarter of the probability in state A moves to B: one sixth in total. Half of the B probability moves to A: also one sixth. Equal probability moves both ways, so the distribution stays the same.

That is a stationary distribution. It does not mean the dot stops moving. It means the chances of finding it in A or B do not change.

Will a different starting point approach this balance? Start in state A with probability one. After one step, the chance of A is three quarters. After two steps, it is eleven sixteenths, closer to two thirds.

Call the current chance of A, p. Next time, we keep three quarters of p, and gain half of the remaining probability. That is one half plus one quarter of p. Subtract two thirds from both sides: the gap from balance becomes one quarter as large each step.

So this chain approaches the same balance from any starting probability. This conclusion uses these transition rules; not every Markov chain settles. The motion can continue while the proportions become steady.
